card.hook: From the middle of Metekhi Bridge, Narikala looks like it's perched right on top of the Old Town rooftops, with the river sliding past underneath and Metekhi Church in front. It's a postcard, and you're allowed to take it.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of Metekhi Bridge, looking upstream toward the fortress. The main body of the walls lies to the south-west, so face that way for your main shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the walls and the church. Go to zoom 0.5x for the whole sweep of stonework, then zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single tower or the rooftops below.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line a wall or tower up with one so the stonework stays straight, then keep a bit of sky above it.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or in the hour before sunset, when the light is softer and the stone looks warmer. Midday sun can wash the sky out.
card.selfie_here: Head to Abanotubani and stand with the brick bath domes in front of you, so the fortress walls on the ridge rise behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the walls fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the flat plateau of the Tabori Monastery viewpoint, about halfway up the hill above Abanotubani, and frame you with the fortress across the gorge.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay off the closed sections of the walls: they're work sites with loose stone and long drops. Access can change, so check what's open when you arrive. Photography isn't allowed inside St Nicholas Church.
card.challenge: Take a few steps between every shot and see if you can get three completely different Narikalas from one slope.
card.good_to_know: A fortress has stood here since about the year 364, though most of the stonework you see dates from the 16th and 17th centuries. An earthquake in 1827 damaged parts of it, and those parts were later pulled down. The church of St Nicholas in the lower court was built in 1996-1997 to replace a 13th-century church lost to fire.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the middle of Metekhi Bridge, looking upstream toward the fortress. The main body of the walls lies to the south-west, so face that way for your main shot.

card.hook: Here's a funny thing about Metekhi Church: the best view from its terrace is of everything except the church. You get Old Town rooftops, the river and a bronze king on a horse, and it's a great trade.
card.stand_here: Walk to the churchyard terrace on the cliff edge, right beside the King Vakhtang Gorgasali statue, and face across the river to the Old Town. Want the church itself in the shot? Head to Metekhi Bridge and look back at it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the big terrace view, then try 0.5x to squeeze the statue and the rooftops into one frame. If your phone has zoom 2x or 5x, use it to pick out the domed sulphur baths.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the statue on one third of the frame and let the river and rooftops fill the rest.
card.best_time: Late afternoon gives you lovely warm light. Early morning is quieter if you like having the terrace to yourself.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera on the cliff-edge terrace next to the bronze horseman, with the statue and the river view behind you. Switch to 0.5x so more of the scene fits in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a shot with the church cliff rising above you, go down to the riverside embankment at river level at the Rike Park end, and ask a passer-by to take your photo from there.
card.rules_and_safety: The terrace is open-air and free, but the church is a place of worship, so dress modestly (shoulders and knees covered, head covering for women). Skip the flash, ask before photographing worshippers, and check on site whether photos inside are allowed.
card.challenge: Hold your phone low and close to the statue so the king towers over the whole Old Town, then see if your friends can name the horse's best side.
card.good_to_know: The church you see today mostly dates from 1278 to 1289, in the reign of King Demetrius II. Oral tradition traces the site back to the 5th century, though there's no firm evidence for that. It's small, about 20 by 16 metres, and has been a prison, a store for museum collections and a youth theatre in the 1970s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the churchyard terrace on the cliff edge, right beside the King Vakhtang Gorgasali statue, and face across the river to the Old Town. Want the church itself in the shot? Head to Metekhi Bridge and look back at it.

card.hook: A shiny gold St George is stabbing a dragon in the middle of a roundabout, and the traffic just carries on around him like it's Tuesday. Honestly, it's a great show.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement of Rustaveli Avenue, the tree-lined main street, and look east towards Freedom Square. The gold column sits at the end of the street like it's waiting for you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the monument with its setting. Go 0.5x if you want more trees and buildings, but keep the column away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched. Try 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for a closer shot of the statue.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the column on the central vertical line, then let the trees run down both sides to lead the eye to it.
card.best_time: After dark is the showstopper, when the column is lit. Early morning is quieter, so you'll get a clearer view along the avenue.
card.selfie_here: Try the pavements around the edge of the square, or the start of Rustaveli Avenue where it meets the roundabout. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the column over your shoulder. Check on the spot that it really is behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the start of Rustaveli Avenue and frame you against the column, with the avenue as your backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a busy roundabout, so shoot from the pavements and use the pedestrian crossings or underground passages. Keep your phone and bag close, as guides warn about pickpockets. The square can be crowded or closed during state events.
card.challenge: Get the column dead centre on the line with not a single stranger's head in the frame. Patience wins this one.
card.good_to_know: A big statue of Lenin stood here from 1956 until it was symbolically pulled down in August 1991. Zurab Tsereteli's St George was unveiled in the same spot on 23 November 2006. The square got its name in 1918, and six streets branch out from it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement of Rustaveli Avenue, the tree-lined main street, and look east towards Freedom Square. The gold column sits at the end of the street like it's waiting for you.

card.hook: Picture a Ferris wheel perched right on the edge of a mountain, with the whole of Tbilisi spread out behind it. That's Mtatsminda Park, and it's the rare fairground where the view is as good as the rides.
card.stand_here: Head to Mtatsminda View Point, the big viewing deck along the front of the Restaurant Funicular building. Face the city, with the park behind you, and step a few paces either way if a ride gets in the way.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the rides and the view together. Go to 0.5x when you want the whole wheel and the city in one frame, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out rooftops far below.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, and keep your phone level so the wheel doesn't look like it's leaning.
card.best_time: Go late afternoon into evening, when the light is softer and the city lights start to come on. Midday is still good for bright, colourful ride shots, but the distant view can look a bit flat.
card.selfie_here: Stand inside the wooden tree-shaped structure at the park entrance and face back toward the TV tower. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the tower loom over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos aren't allowed inside the park's buildings, but you can photograph the grounds and the view. Rides may need tickets, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the Giant Wheel and the rooftops below in one frame, then zoom in and grab one tiny detail you'd have missed.
card.good_to_know: The park sits about 770 metres up, the highest point in Tbilisi, and covers more than 100 hectares. The Giant Wheel is 65 metres tall and takes 10 to 12 minutes for one turn. The funicular from Chonkadze Street opened in 1905, and the park itself was founded in the 1930s, in the Soviet period.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Mtatsminda View Point, the big viewing deck along the front of the Restaurant Funicular building. Face the city, with the park behind you, and step a few paces either way if a ride gets in the way.

card.hook: Sameba's gold dome pops up over the old rooftops of Tbilisi like it's playing peekaboo, and you can spot it from a long way off. The trick is to stop shooting it head-on and use the Old Town to frame it.
card.stand_here: Head to Betlemi Street in the Old Town and look for the stretch with the restaurant balcony. Face up toward the cathedral so the gilt dome sits behind the balcony.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the balcony and the dome both fit in one picture, and don't zoom in too tight. Then zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for a second, closer shot of the dome and cross.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the dome on an upper intersection, tap it, then slide a little darker so the gold doesn't glare and the sky stays blue.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon or evening. One guide warns that midday light is glary on all that gold.
card.selfie_here: Go to the north-western side of the big square at the base of the cathedral, by the glass enclosure holding St. Nino's Cross. Face west toward Old Tbilisi, then hold your front camera up so the cathedral sits over your shoulder. Try 0.5x to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: On the approach road up from Avlabari metro station, ask a passer-by to stand below you and look up, so the whole tall facade fits in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine outside and in the grounds, but they're restricted inside the main nave, especially during services, and you should skip the flash. Check posted signs and the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the balcony and the golden dome in one shot with the cathedral standing perfectly straight, no leaning allowed.
card.good_to_know: Sameba is the main cathedral of the Georgian Orthodox Church and the third-tallest Eastern Orthodox cathedral anywhere. It stands 86.1 metres to the top of its gilded cross, and the cross alone is 7.5 metres. It was built from 1995 to 2004 on Elia Hill, designed by Archil Mindiashvili, and consecrated on 23 November 2004.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Betlemi Street in the Old Town and look for the stretch with the restaurant balcony. Face up toward the cathedral so the gilt dome sits behind the balcony.

card.hook: Meet the host of Tbilisi: a 20-metre aluminium woman who greets friends with a bowl of wine and enemies with a sword. She stands on top of Sololaki hill, looking out over the whole city.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map, right at the statue on the viewing platform at her feet, and take your first photos there facing her and the Old Town. Then walk a few steps back so the whole figure fits in with the skyline behind her.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x on the platform to fit the statue and the skyline into one frame. Back at zoom 1x, a few steps away, she looks more natural. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the wine bowl, the sword and the rooftops below.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the statue, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Late afternoon around golden hour, or early morning, as guides suggest. Both are calmer, softer-light times of day, and one guide says the sunset view from the platform is especially nice.
card.selfie_here: Use the small viewing platform at her base, where one review calls the perspective unique. Switch to the front camera and check how much of her fits behind you. She's very tall, so step back if she gets cut off.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the viewing balcony on the approach, just before you reach the monument, so the whole figure fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: One guide advises you to beware of crowds and occasional scammers at the site. Space in front of the statue is limited and the top can get busy, so be patient and shoot when people move away.
card.challenge: Get three shots: a close-up of the wine bowl, a close-up of the sword, and one wide shot with the whole city behind her. Then pick which one is the friend and which is the enemy.
card.good_to_know: The monument went up in 1958, when Tbilisi celebrated its 1500th anniversary, and was designed by the sculptor Elguja Amashukeli. The wine bowl is for friends and the sword is for enemies. The statue you see today replaced the earlier one in 1997.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map, right at the statue on the viewing platform at her feet, and take your first photos there facing her and the Old Town. Then walk a few steps back so the whole figure fits in with the skyline behind her.

card.hook: Legend says a king's falcon dropped out of the sky here and landed Tbilisi its hot springs. Today the bathhouse roofs huddle below a fortress hill, and the whole scene fits on your phone screen.
card.stand_here: Head for იოსებ გრიშაშვილის ქუჩა and stand about 70 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, then face south-east. Stop wherever the lane opens up enough to show the roofs with the hillside behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit roofs, lane and hillside in one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for doorways and rooflines.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the building walls straight, and if the sky goes white, tap it and drag the slider to make the picture a little darker.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people in the lanes. Evening brings warm street light, and night mode helps once it gets dark.
card.selfie_here: Go to the falcon and pheasant fountain beside the blue-tiled Orbeliani (Chreli Abano) bathhouse and stand with the facade behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low so the blue tiles fit over your shoulder. You can also pose on Abano Street right in front of the patterned blue front.
card.ask_someone: For a shot of yourself with the whole bath district behind you, stand on Metekhi Bridge, on the far side of the river, and ask a passer-by to frame it (it's a 10-12 minute walk from the baths).
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the baths, photography may be restricted, so keep your phone in the locker, don't photograph other people and don't film the public hall. Don't peer down through the dome openings either, because they open onto the baths. Bathhouses are businesses, so check the official site of any bath before you go.
card.challenge: Get one wide shot with a strip of fortress hill above the roofs, then hunt down three small details: a doorway, some brickwork and a street corner.
card.good_to_know: Abanotubani means 'bath district', and it sits on the east bank of the Mtkvari River at the foot of Narikala fortress. Local legend says King Vakhtang Gorgasali's falcon fell here, he found the warm water and decided to found a new capital on the spot. By the end of the 13th century the city had 65 baths.

card.hook: Picture a glass-and-steel sea creature stretched across the Kura River, glowing after dark. That's the Bridge of Peace, and people in Tbilisi still argue about it. Whichever side you're on, it's a great photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Baratashvili Bridge, halfway across on the left-hand side if you're walking from the Rike Park side toward the Old Town. Face upriver so the Bridge of Peace is straight ahead of you with the Old Town buildings rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole curve of the canopy into one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural view along the walkway. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) pulls in Narikala Fortress or Metekhi Church behind the bridge.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the line of the walkway on one of them so the curve leads the eye in, and keep the horizon level because the canopy makes a crooked frame obvious.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the lights are on. They run from 90 minutes before sunset until 90 minutes after sunrise. The canopy changes its pattern every hour, so take a few frames over a full hour. Just after sunset, while the sky still has some colour, is a lovely moment.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x so you and the bridge both fit, and hold the phone a little higher than your face. Turn so the glowing canopy sits over your shoulder, then take a few shots, because the lights keep changing.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the left-hand pavement near the middle of Baratashvili Bridge, facing upriver, while you stand in front of them so you're between them and the Bridge of Peace.
card.rules_and_safety: Cross Baratashvili Bridge using the underground pedestrian passage at its end, because cars on the slip lane make crossing at street level quite dangerous. The Bridge of Peace is an open pedestrian bridge, but check the official site before you go in case of any works or closures.
card.challenge: Catch one walker on the bridge so they look tiny against the curve, and see if you can make them look like they're strolling through the belly of a whale.
card.good_to_know: The Bridge of Peace opened on 6 May 2010 and is about 150 metres long. Italian architect Michele De Lucchi designed it. After dark its canopy carries 1,208 LED fixtures running four lighting programmes, and one of them makes the roof twinkle like stars.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Baratashvili Bridge, halfway across on the left-hand side if you're walking from the Rike Park side toward the Old Town. Face upriver so the Bridge of Peace is straight ahead of you with the Old Town buildings rising behind it.

ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand on the left-hand pavement near the midpoint of the bridge and face upriver, so the Bridge of Peace is directly ahead and the visitor can stand between you and the bridge. The Old Town buildings are also in view. Sunset is suggested as the best time.

The Baratashvili Bridge suggestion is a passer-by photo spot based on a guide's described view, not a page-confirmed camera position, so check it on arrival. The Bridge of Peace's LED lights switch on about 90 minutes before sunset according to one guide, and sources disagree on how many LEDs there are. No page I found gives rules on selfie sticks or tripods for this site.

card.hook: After dark, Tbilisi's grandest street turns into a single glowing line in a sea of city lights, and you can see all of it from a hilltop. It's the kind of view that makes you go quiet for a second, then reach for your phone.
card.stand_here: Head up to Mtatsminda Park, the hilltop park above Rustaveli Avenue (the cable car leaves from behind the Academy of Sciences). Face out over the city, with the avenue below you as a line among the lights.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to take in the city and the glow of the avenue. Then try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone, to pick out the line of Rustaveli Street. Save zoom 0.5x for when you want the whole hillside and skyline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and night mode, brace your elbows on a wall or railing, tap the brightest part of the city, then slide the brightness down a touch so the lights don't blow out.
card.best_time: Go in the evening, after dark, when the avenue shows up among the city lights. That's when the view really works.
card.selfie_here: Back down on the avenue, stand by the small fountain on the Parliament forecourt (Shota Rustaveli Ave 8) with the building directly behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x so the old facade fills the background, and hold the phone a little high.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far pavement in front of Kashveti Church, facing the Parliament's arched facade, while you pose by the fountain on the forecourt.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine in public spaces along the avenue, but watch for 'no photography' signs inside museums and private places. The Parliament isn't open to visitors, so shoot its facade from across the avenue. One reviewer says the avenue has no traffic lights or pedestrian crossings, so use the underground passages to cross. The cable car is a paid ride, so check it's running before you go. Works on the avenue were due to close it to traffic until the end of 2026, so parts may be fenced off.
card.challenge: Find Rustaveli Street among the lights, then put it on a lower gridline and see if you can leave a little sky above it.
card.good_to_know: Rustaveli Avenue was laid out in the 1840s on the orders of the Russian viceroy Mikhail Vorontsov, who wanted to give a Persian-style city a more European feel. It got its present name, after the medieval poet Shota Rustaveli, in 1918. The cable car to the hill opened in 1959, closed in 1990 and reopened in October 2024.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head up to Mtatsminda Park, the hilltop park above Rustaveli Avenue (the cable car leaves from behind the Academy of Sciences). Face out over the city, with the avenue below you as a line among the lights.

card.hook: Don't expect a big sweeping view here. Anchiskhati hides in a tangle of narrow old streets, and the fun is in the brick, the carved stone and the little details. Think treasure hunt, not postcard.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ioane Shavteli Street, just south of the church, and look at the eastern side as you walk along the street. The relief of the Exaltation of the Cross and the brick bell tower fit in one photo, with the street leading your eye to them. Keep to the side so people and vehicles can pass.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole facade and the street. Then try zoom 2x to pick out the relief and the top of the bell tower. In the tight courtyard gateway, zoom 0.5x helps, but keep the arch straight so the lines don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and use the edges of the street as lines pointing to the church, with the bell tower standing straight up.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, when warm light falls on the western face of the bell tower, according to one guide. Check where the shade falls on the eastern facade before you pick your shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the church yard garden at 11 Ioane Shavteli St, on or near the garden benches outside the building. Reviewers call it a good spot for pictures, with sculptures and scenic corners. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) and tilt so the church is over your shoulder. Nobody says the basilica is perfectly framed there, so check the view on your screen first.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Ioane Shavteli Street, the approach to the church, while you stand in front of the eastern facade so the relief and brick bell tower are behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside is officially prohibited, so stick to exterior shots, or ask staff first. It's a working church, so skip photos during services, never photograph worshippers, and don't use flash. Women are expected to cover their heads.
card.challenge: Find the Exaltation of the Cross relief and get it into one frame with the bell tower, without any wobbly, leaning lines.
card.good_to_know: Anchiskhati is the oldest surviving church in Tbilisi, and the Georgian annals credit King Dachi of Iberia (around 522-534) with building it. It got its name in 1675, when a treasured icon of the Saviour was brought to Tbilisi to keep it safe from an Ottoman invasion. The brick belfry dates from the same year, and a restoration in the 1950s and 60s brought the church back to its seventeenth-century look.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ioane Shavteli Street, just south of the church, and look at the eastern side as you walk along the street. The relief of the Exaltation of the Cross and the brick bell tower fit in one photo, with the street leading your eye to them. Keep to the side so people and vehicles can pass.

card.hook: Pale yellow stone, a bell tower standing on its own, and Old Town rooftops packed in all around: Sioni Cathedral gives you a proper 'I was in Tbilisi' shot in a single frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on Sioni Street, in the lane to the south of the church, and face the bell tower so it rises above the Old Town roofline. This spot is approximate, so shuffle a few steps either way until the tower sits cleanly above the roofs.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the church and its surroundings together. Then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pull the tower closer. In the courtyard, switch to 0.5x to fit the church and tower in together.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the bell tower on one vertical line with rooftops filling the bottom of the frame, and tap the tower, then slide darker if the sky is bright so the pale stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Going early may help you avoid crowds. Soft light early or late in the day tends to flatter the stone.
card.selfie_here: Try the courtyard beside the bell tower: use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the tower stands up behind your shoulder. The courtyard is quiet, with benches and old trees, so it's a calm place to take your time.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand in the lane south of the cathedral, framing the bell tower against the Old Town roofline, and step back a little so more of the scene fits in.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working church, so be discreet around worshippers and don't photograph people while they pray. Photography inside is generally allowed without flash, but rules can change and may be restricted during services, so follow the signs and the cathedral's instructions.
card.challenge: Can you get the bell tower sitting neatly on a gridline with a full row of rooftops underneath, and no leaning walls?
card.good_to_know: Sioni takes its name from Mount Zion in Jerusalem and has been rebuilt many times since the 6th and 7th centuries. The building you see today is based on a 13th-century version, with changes between the 17th and 19th centuries. The three-storey bell tower dates from a rebuilding in 1425, was largely destroyed in 1795 and was restored in 1939.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Sioni Street, in the lane to the south of the church, and face the bell tower so it rises above the Old Town roofline. This spot is approximate, so shuffle a few steps either way until the tower sits cleanly above the roofs.

card.hook: Right behind Narikala Fortress, a whole wooded gorge is hiding, and it has a waterfall running down the middle. You don't need a long climb to get the classic view of it.
card.stand_here: Go to the panoramic lookout just left of the main entrance gate. Stand about 310 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. You'll see the gorge and the waterfall with the garden's trees framing both sides.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole gorge in, then switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched view. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the waterfall itself.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the waterfall, then slide it a little darker so the bright water and sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives the softest light. The gorge goes into shadow early, so don't leave your main photos until just before closing time.
card.selfie_here: Head for the white arched bridge above the Tsavkisistskali waterfall. Two blogs call the bridge-over-waterfall view a good selfie backdrop, so use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a bit low so the gorge sits behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At the viewing platform at the bottom of the waterfall steps, stand facing the waterfall and hand your phone to a friendly passer-by.
card.rules_and_safety: The steps down to the waterfall can be slippery, so hold the railing. The garden is a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go for current ticket rules and opening times.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the waterfall on one vertical line, and let branches fill the top corners like a leafy picture frame.
card.good_to_know: The garden covers 161 hectares and holds more than 4,500 plant groups. A French traveller, Jean Chardin, described royal gardens on this site in 1671, and it became an official botanical garden in 1845. In 2018 it gained new walking and cycling lanes.

card.hook: You're strolling down a tree-lined avenue, and then a striped, turreted building with horseshoe arches pops into view, looking like it wandered in from somewhere far more exotic. That's the Opera and Ballet Theatre, and it's a great one to record.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement across Rustaveli Avenue from the theatre's main front, and face north-west. You'll see the whole front with its arches, striped stonework and turrets, framed by the stone buildings along the avenue.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from across the avenue. If the whole front won't fit, tap 0.5x and keep your phone level so the building doesn't lean. Save zoom 2x for close-ups of the arches and stripes.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them, so the turrets stand up straight.
card.best_time: Go in the evening, when the facade is lit. If it looks too bright on your screen, slide it a little darker so the glowing stonework keeps its detail, and use night mode if the light is low.
card.selfie_here: Try the fountain beside the theatre on Rustaveli Avenue, where the facade is reflected in the water. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement across the avenue so the full arches fit in the frame, while you pose in front of the theatre.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside, photo rules depend on the moment: check the official site first, skip the flash, and don't take photos during a performance.
card.challenge: Can you catch all the turrets and both ends of the stripy front in one straight, gridline-perfect shot, without the building leaning?
card.good_to_know: The company was founded in 1851, and it has been in this Neo-Moorish building, designed by Victor Schröter, since 1896. Inside, the layout is that of a typical European opera house, so the Oriental look is all in the decoration. Fires damaged the theatre several times, and the latest restoration finished in January 2016 after six years of work.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement across Rustaveli Avenue from the theatre's main front, and face north-west. You'll see the whole front with its arches, striped stonework and turrets, framed by the stone buildings along the avenue.

card.hook: The Tbilisi TV Tower is a slim red-and-white mast on top of a mountain, so it looks tall before you even count the hill under it. Lucky for you, that makes it a very easy thing to photograph.
card.stand_here: Head for the park ground south-west of the tower on the Mtatsminda Park plateau. The tower is about 264 m to the north-east of it, so face north-east and the mast will be right there in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole mast and some of the park in the frame, then switch to 1x for a calmer view with the city below. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pick out the top of the tower against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the mast up with a vertical line, then tap the sky or the tower and slide it a little darker so the sky stays rich and the lit tower doesn't glow out.
card.best_time: Go in the evening, when the tower is lit. Give yourself a few minutes to walk around the park, because the mast looks quite different when you change distance.
card.selfie_here: Try the long row of terraces at the top of Mtatsminda Park, looking east over the valley with the tower on the summit behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the tower over your shoulder with the city behind you.
card.ask_someone: For a shot of you with the tower across the view, ask someone on the path behind Narikala Fortress (heading toward Mother of Georgia and the National Botanical Garden) to take it while you stand in front, and check the framing before they hand the phone back.
card.rules_and_safety: There are no photography restrictions from public areas in Mtatsminda Park. Don't plan on going inside the tower, and check on the day. Avoid isolated spots like the TV Tower trails after dark; Mtatsminda Park itself is generally safe after dark.
card.challenge: Get the whole mast standing perfectly straight on a gridline, with a bit of park path at the bottom so it looks like it's growing out of the ground.
card.good_to_know: The tower was built in 1972 and replaced an earlier tower from 1955, which was moved to the area near Gori. It is 274.5 m high. It stands on a mountain 719.2 m above sea level.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the park ground south-west of the tower on the Mtatsminda Park plateau. The tower is about 264 m to the north-east of it, so face north-east and the mast will be right there in front of you.

card.hook: Here's a nice bonus: this museum sits right on Rustaveli Avenue, Tbilisi's main street, so your photo shows the building and the city buzzing around it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement right at the phone icon on the map, facing the building. Then step back along the pavement as far as is safe until the whole frontage fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the building. If the pavement is tight and you can't fit it all in, try 0.5x. Then use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a close shot of the entrance and facade details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building's edges up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Daylight is easiest for a clear shot of the outside. Earlier in the day the pavement is usually quieter, so you get a cleaner frame. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing.
card.selfie_here: Try the front steps of the Georgian National Museum on the Rustaveli Avenue side, near Freedom Square, with the stone facade behind you. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x if you want more of the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the avenue pavement facing the building, while you stand on the front steps, so the steps and the full facade fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash is often not allowed inside, so check the signs at the entrance or ask staff before you take photos in the galleries. The exhibition remembers victims of political repression, so a calm, respectful photo suits it best.
card.challenge: Take one clean wide shot of the whole frontage, with no parked car, sign or passer-by cutting into the edges of the building.
card.good_to_know: The Museum of the Soviet Occupation opened on 26 May 2006, Georgia's Independence Day. It tells the story of the Soviet years in Georgia, from 1921 to 1991. The permanent exhibition has around 3,000 items, including archive documents, photographs, video and objects from Soviet-era prison cells.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement right at the phone icon on the map, facing the building. Then step back along the pavement as far as is safe until the whole frontage fits.

card.hook: You're climbing Botanikuri Street past the sulphur baths, and then a red-brick minaret pops up at the top with a cliff right behind it. It looks like a film set, and you didn't even have to look for it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Botanikuri Street, walking uphill from the sulphur baths, near the top of the street. The mosque is just to the south-west of you, so face south-west and look straight along the street at the brick walls and the minaret.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the mosque, the minaret and the slope behind all fit in one shot. Then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) for the minaret top, the arched windows and the mosaics. Use 0.5x only if you step closer and want the whole facade, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the minaret on one of the vertical lines, then tap the brick wall and drag the brightness slider a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out and the red stays rich.
card.best_time: Try soft morning or late-afternoon light, which tends to be kind to brick and mosaics. The street is also at its quietest then, so you get a cleaner shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the pavement in front of the tiled bathhouse front (the Orbeliani baths) right next to the mosque on Botanikuri Street. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and step back until the minaret fits over your shoulder, but check the frame before you smile because the mosque may not line up from every spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Botanikuri Street (No. 32) on the approach from the lower streets, far enough back to take in the whole facade and minaret, while you stand in front of the red-brick exterior.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship, so photograph the exterior from the street, and ask permission before shooting inside or any worshippers. Dress modestly if you go in, and check access before you go, because it may not always be open to visitors.
card.challenge: Get the minaret perfectly on a gridline with the cliff behind it, then find one mosaic or brick detail that nobody else on the street is photographing.
card.good_to_know: This is the only mosque still standing in Tbilisi's historic Old Town, and it mixes Neo-Gothic and Islamic details. The current red-brick building dates from 1895 and was restored in 1998. Sunni and Shia Muslims pray here together, which is unusual.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Botanikuri Street, walking uphill from the sulphur baths, near the top of the street. The mosque is just to the south-west of you, so face south-west and look straight along the street at the brick walls and the minaret.

card.hook: Everyone photographs Kashveti Church from the busy avenue out front. Slip round the back instead, and you get the stonework and the dome with far less fuss.
card.stand_here: Stand in the park called 9 აპრილის პარკი, directly behind the church. Face south-west, with the church's rear and dome ahead of you, and walk around a little to check the framing, since it isn't a classic viewpoint.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 2x to pick out the rear of the church and its dome. Switch to zoom 1x for a wider shot that includes the trees and the park around it.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the church, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out the pale stone.
card.best_time: Morning light is usually kinder to the stonework. The best direction can vary, so check how the light falls when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: Try the little garden on the south side of the church, facing the carved stone exterior. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x with the church behind your shoulder. This spot is our best guess rather than a known selfie spot, so check it on the ground.
card.ask_someone: For a shot of you with the Parliament building behind, ask a passer-by to take it on the avenue side of the church's main facade, and stay off the busy pavement edge.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an active place of worship, so be quiet and respectful, use no flash, and ask before photographing inside. Guides say photography is generally allowed, but one visitor reported a ban and a dress code, so check on arrival. Ask politely before photographing people, including at weddings.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the dome on a vertical line, and tuck a tree branch into the corner of the frame.
card.good_to_know: The church was built between 1904 and 1910 by architect Leopold Bilfeldt, who modelled it on the medieval Samtavisi Cathedral. It replaced an older brick church from 1753. Lado Gudiashvili painted the frescoes inside in 1947, and the name comes from Georgian words for 'stone' and 'to give birth'.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the park called 9 აპრილის პარკი, directly behind the church. Face south-west, with the church's rear and dome ahead of you, and walk around a little to check the framing, since it isn't a classic viewpoint.

card.hook: This church doesn't look polished, and that's the charm. Surb Nshan has weathered walls and the worn look of a building with a long story, so photograph it just as you find it.
card.stand_here: Head for the spot near ვერცხლის I ჩიხი, about 30 m north-west of the subject (that's the phone icon on the map). Face south-east and the church is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole building and the ground around it. Squeezed for space? Zoom 0.5x gets it all in. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for stonework, doorways and the roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the walls and roof up with them, so the church stands nice and straight.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when soft daylight shows off the stone texture. Harsh midday sun flattens the walls and turns the damaged patches dark.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and keep the church over your shoulder so more of it fits in. Stay on open public ground, and take a few frames to get one where you both look good.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is damaged and may be closed or fenced off, so check local information before you go. Stay on open public ground and keep to any barriers or signs.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot, then find a door, window or damaged wall and get a close-up that tells the church's story.
card.good_to_know: Surb Nshan, also called the Church of the Holy Seal, is an Armenian church in Old Tbilisi. It was built between 1703 and 1711 and reconstructed in 1780. Arson partially destroyed it in 2002, and it still looks dilapidated.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the spot near ვერცხლის I ჩიხი, about 30 m north-west of the subject (that's the phone icon on the map). Face south-east and the church is right in front of you.

selfie_research.safety: The Wikipedia list of Armenian churches in Tbilisi describes the Church of the Holy Seal (Surb Nshan) as at risk of collapse, with its interior burned by arsonists.
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with Surb Nshan behind the visitor, or a named spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole church. Reinisfischer's blog mentions only a tower shot 'from nearby street' without naming the street. The only named location near the church is the crossroads of Akopyan and Serebryanaya streets, near Erekle II Square; a page places the church there, but it does not say it is a photo position, so I did not use it. Wander-Lush calls the church Insta-famous but names no photo spot. Wikimedia Commons has camera coordinates for church photos (about 41.6894, 44.8085 and 41.6943, 44.8047), but those are bare coordinates, not named places, so I did not use them. No page I found mentions selfie-stick or tripod rules. Sources also disagree on the name: Tripadvisor uses 'Church of the Holy Sign', while Commons and Wikipedia use 'Holy Seal'. The Tripadvisor 'Holy Sign' listing address is Vertskhlis st 23.
